summary: Greendale officials, led by Mayor Linda Matheson, announced a phased overhaul of the town's parks and playgrounds, unveiled as the Neighborhood Improvement Plans on September 15, 2023. The project uses public-private partnerships and emphasizes sustainability, inclusive playgrounds, smart technology, community gardens, safety, cultural events, health, and nature conservation. Phase One begins November 1 at Hathaway Park, with further plans to convert abandoned lots into pocket parks.
one_line: Greendale launches a phased, partnership-funded upgrade of its parks and playgrounds, starting with Hathaway Park on November 1, focusing on sustainability, inclusivity, technology and community.
key_facts: Mayor Linda Matheson unveiled the Neighborhood Improvement Plans on September 15, 2023, at a press conference at City Hall.

By October 2023, Henderson's Hardware Emporium and the tech start-up InnovateX, along with venture capitalists, had pledged funding and expertise, allowing the project to proceed without burdening taxpayers.
Phase One is expected to begin by November 1 at Hathaway Park, the oldest park in Greendale.
Sarah Kingston, Director of Public Works, oversees the operations of the project.
Sustainability measures include solar-powered lights and water-conserving irrigation systems; landscape architect Michael Thompson handles the greenery.
Educator James P. Sullivan advises on playground designs that are inclusive and ADA-compliant, with interactive installations.
Elijah Patel, the youngest member of the city council, proposed smart benches with charging stations and free Wi-Fi.
Plots within the parks will be allocated to residents for community gardens; environmental activist Claire Rodriguez supports the idea.
Safety plans include state-of-the-art surveillance systems and increased patrols by community security teams, with Police Chief Daniel Abrams collaborating with the Parks Department.
By January 2024, the Parks and Recreation Committee expects to roll out a calendar of outdoor concerts, movie nights, and fitness classes.
Economist David Nguyen says quality public spaces stimulate economic activity; the project is expected to create construction jobs and raise property values and consumer spending.
New fitness zones with outdoor gym equipment are planned, praised by pediatrician Dr. Anthony Price.
Plans include expanding natural trails and protecting indigenous flora and fauna, with biologist Sandra Clark involved in the conservation strategy.
Further plans include repurposing abandoned lots into pocket parks and community spaces.
